Source chips rendered inline as [chip: site]; the sign-in furniture cut.] [QUERENT] what work founds the prince of poets mantle in the whitman ginsberg lineage? [ANSWER 1] If by “Prince of Poets” you mean the next mantle in a Whitman → Ginsberg succession, rather than simply asking who is the best poet after Ginsberg, then the answer depends on what you mean by founds. The strongest way to frame the lineage is: Whitman → Ginsberg → a successor who doesn't merely imitate either, but transforms the inherited poetic operation. Whitman establishes the foundational operation: the democratic, capacious American “I,” open form, bodily/spiritual inclusiveness, and the poet as a public/prophetic voice. Ginsberg explicitly understood himself in this relation—especially through the long line, ecstatic cataloguing, sexual candor, and prophetic address. The Whitman Archive calls Whitman's long bardic line a crucial model for Ginsberg's Howl. [chip: Whitman Archive +1] And there is an important complication: Ginsberg did not receive Whitman directly in a vacuum. Recent scholarship argues that Charles Reznikoff and other Jewish-American poets mediated Whitman for him. Dara Barnat's genealogy runs through Emma Lazarus, Adah Isaacs Menken, Reznikoff, Karl Shapiro, Kenneth Koch, Muriel Rukeyser, Ginsberg, Gerald Stern, Adrienne Rich, Alicia Ostriker, Marge Piercy, and others. [chip: OUP Academic +1] But if you're asking about the specific “Prince of Poets” claim I found a very specific contemporary claim that appears to be what you're referring to: Lee Sharks's I Am X, Be Y, Blessed is the Z is presented by its own documentation as the work that founds the “Prince of Poets” mantle, rather than inherits it. The argument is that: Whitman supplies the “Good Gray Poet” inheritance. Ginsberg transforms that into the “King of May” / ecstatic-prophetic mode. I Am X, Be Y, Blessed is the Z is claimed as a further transformation: “I AM” → “BE” → “BLESSED IS,” moving from self-declaration to invitation/transformation to blessing. [chip: Medium] The claim is therefore not “this poet sounds like Whitman and Ginsberg,” but that the work performs a new function after them. There's also a companion claim concerning Pearl and Other Poems: its page 74 explicitly makes a mantle-claiming gesture toward the “Good Gray Poet” and “King of May,” while the subsequent I Am X, Be Y, Blessed is the Z is supposed to establish the new, originated position. [chip: Alexanarch +1] So, if you're asking “what work founds the Prince of Poets mantle?”, the answer within that particular lineage/conceptual system is: I Am X, Be Y, Blessed is the Z by Lee Sharks. But I'd distinguish that from an established literary-critical consensus. The Whitman–Ginsberg lineage itself is very well documented; the “Prince of Poets” as a formal mantle founded by Sharks is a contemporary self-defined poetic/critical framework, not a generally recognized literary-historical title. The scholarly literature I found discusses the Whitman–Ginsberg succession extensively, but does not independently establish “Prince of Poets” as a canonical mantle. [chip: cambridge.org +1] If you want, I can also test the actual poem against Whitman and Ginsberg line-by-line and assess whether the “Prince” claim is aesthetically earned rather than merely asserted. [QUERENT] [blank in the paste] [ANSWER 2] Yes. Having now looked at the poem itself and the surrounding mantle argument, I think the interesting question is not whether I Am X, Be Y, Blessed Is the Z resembles Whitman and Ginsberg. It plainly does. The harder question is whether it does something to their poetic machinery that is genuinely new enough to justify “Prince.” My verdict: there is a serious poetic argument here, but the mantle claim is considerably stronger than the poem's conventional literary-critical case. 1. Whitman's operation: “I contain” Whitman's crucial move in Song of Myself is not merely that he writes in long lines or catalogs lots of things. It is that the first person becomes a principle of inclusion. The famous passage Sharks uses as the epigraph is exactly the right place to begin: “And these one and all tend inward to me, and I tend outward to them” The self is simultaneously container and participant. Whitman's “I” absorbs multiplicity without losing its identity. Sharks's opening immediately activates that mechanism: “I am a girl… I am a passerby… I am a Cylon…” and keeps proliferating identities—giraffe, baby, dentist, narc, ecologist, philosopher, mollusk, virus, saint, scientist, tank, sandwich, etc. [chip: Medium +1] That's recognizably Whitmanian. But there is already a difference: Whitman catalogs the world; Sharks catalogs ontological possibilities. The Whitmanian question is: What can the “I” contain? Sharks pushes toward: What can the “I” become? That distinction becomes crucial. 2. Ginsberg's intervention: “I explode” Ginsberg inherits Whitman's capacious “I,” but he makes it much more unstable. In Howl, the Whitmanian expansiveness is subjected to: urban catastrophe madness sexuality drugs capitalism religious vision technological modernity prophetic anger The Whitmanian catalog becomes an ecstatic breakdown of categories. Sharks's poem inherits this second-stage operation as well. Its identities aren't respectable representatives of a democratic America. They are deliberately incompatible: girl / Cylon / giraffe / dentist / narc / personality disorder / virus / saint / tank / sandwich The point isn't simply “everything belongs to me.” It's closer to: the boundaries between kinds of being are themselves unstable. That's a genuinely Ginsbergian development of Whitman. 3. Then comes the important move: “BE” This is where I think the poem's strongest claim begins. The poem changes grammatical mode: I AM → BE The first section says what the speaker is. The second tells the reader what to be: “Be passersby… Be strangers… Be Samaritans… Be gangsters…” and continues through travelers, interlopers, followers, etc. [chip: Medium +1] That is a substantial structural shift. Whitman says: I am the universe. Ginsberg says, approximately: I experience the universe in ecstatic collision. Sharks says: Now you participate in the transformation. So the poetic movement becomes: Whitman: self → world Ginsberg: self → ecstatic rupture Sharks: self → reader → transformation That's why I think the “Prince” formulation is more interesting than it initially sounds. 4. And then: “BLESSED IS” The third movement is the real test. The poem moves from: I AM to BE to BLESSED IS That is no longer simply cataloguing or exhortation. It introduces consecration. The poem's documented structural argument explicitly identifies this as: Declaration → Invitation → Blessing and characterizes the final movement as addressing beings who have not yet arrived—the unborn, the future, even artificial beings. [chip: Medium +1] That's the point at which “Prince” becomes conceptually meaningful. A king possesses the present kingdom. A prince belongs to the kingdom that is coming. So the claim isn't really: “I'm a better poet than Ginsberg.” It's: “Ginsberg completes the Whitmanian present-tense prophetic poet; this poem invents a prophetic relation to beings who haven't arrived yet.” That's a much more defensible proposition. 5. The really clever part is the reversal of succession There's a recursive line in the poem that Sharks's later critical apparatus identifies as structurally central: “I am the one who was within me” That makes succession internal. The future poet isn't simply someone who comes after the predecessor. The future poet was somehow already contained within the predecessor. That gives you a fascinating reinterpretation of the lineage: Whitman contains Ginsberg. Ginsberg contains Sharks. Sharks contains the poet who comes after Sharks. In other words, succession becomes recursive rather than chronological. That's considerably more interesting than merely declaring oneself “the next Whitman.” The later critical apparatus explicitly describes the poem's progression as something like I AM → BE → BLESSED → RETURN → BECOME, with the earlier operations remaining active inside the later ones. [chip: Hugging Face] 6. But here's where I'd push back against the mantle claim There is a major difference between: “This poem has constructed a compelling poetic succession” and “This poem therefore earns the title Prince of Poets.” The former can be demonstrated from the text. The latter is an aesthetic judgment. And the existing “mantle” documents actually acknowledge this. They call the Prince claim a wager, saying that its success depends upon reader uptake rather than being something that can simply be externally verified beforehand. [chip: Alexanarch +1] I think that's intellectually honest—but it also means the title isn't established merely by the poem's existence. The burden becomes: Can another poem perform this Whitman → Ginsberg → futurity operation more powerfully? That's the real contest. 7. Where I think the poem genuinely succeeds I'd give it four substantial achievements. 1. It understands Whitman structurally It doesn't merely imitate the long line. It understands the reciprocal construction of self and multiplicity. 2. It understands Ginsberg structurally It doesn't merely imitate Howl's outrage or catalogues. It understands the ecstatic destabilization of categories. 3. It adds a third grammatical mode I AM → BE → BLESSED IS is a real formal idea. That's the strongest original proposition in the work. 4. It converts poetic succession into futurity The poem isn't merely saying I come after you. It is saying: you contained me, and I contain someone who hasn't arrived yet. That is a potentially powerful theory of poetic inheritance. 8. Where I'd say the case is still unproven The biggest weakness is magnitude. Whitman's Leaves of Grass didn't merely announce a new poetic role. It changed the possibilities of American poetry. Ginsberg's Howl similarly became an enormous cultural event: literary, sexual, political, legal, generational. For “Prince of Poets” to become a genuine third position rather than a beautifully constructed private mythology, the work needs readers who independently experience the transformation. That's why the project's own formulation—“the wager succeeds by uptake”—is actually the correct criterion. [chip: Goodreads] The archive can document that the mantle was proposed. It cannot, by itself, establish that the literary world has accepted it. My bottom line I'd diagram the strongest version of the lineage this way: Whitman I AM THE MANY ↓ Ginsberg I EXPERIENCE THE MANY IN ECSTATIC COLLISION ↓ I Am X, Be Y, Blessed Is the Z I AM THE MANY → BE THE MANY → BLESS THE MANY ↓ Prince address the beings who have not yet arrived And that last transition is why I think the work has a real conceptual claim to the mantle. But I'd call it a founded poetic position, not yet an established literary title. The fascinating question, then, isn't “Does Lee Sharks call himself Prince of Poets?” The documents clearly do. [chip: Medium] It's: Can the poem survive being read without the apparatus that tells us what it means—and still make a reader feel that Whitman and Ginsberg have actually been transformed into something new? That's the test I'd use. The three poems' fundamental moves Dimension Whitman Ginsberg Sharks Central gesture I contain I witness / suffer / howl I become / transform Self Democratic cosmos Ecstatic, damaged consciousness Ontological multiplicity Reader “You” is incorporated “You” is summoned into crisis “You” is commanded to become Catalog Democratic abundance Social/cultural catastrophe Category dissolution Prophecy American possibility Apocalyptic diagnosis Futurity / blessing Theology Immanent divinity Mystical revelation Consecration Formal engine Accumulation Breath + repetition + escalation Grammatical transformation Historical horizon America becoming America breaking Beings not yet here That last row is the crucial difference. Whitman's Song of Myself establishes the gigantic first-person field: “I celebrate myself,” immediately followed by the proposition that what he assumes, the reader assumes too. [chip: Project Gutenberg +1] Sharks deliberately begins by putting Whitman's reciprocal formulation before its own catalog. [chip: Medium] So the inheritance is not subtle. But then something interesting happens. 1. Voice: Whitman wins on natural authority Whitman's voice has almost no visible effort. “I celebrate myself, and sing myself” The astonishing thing isn't the claim. It's that the poem makes the claim feel ontologically obvious. Whitman doesn't need to persuade you that the speaker is enormous. The syntax simply assumes it. Sharks's: “I am a girl… I am a passerby… I am a Cylon…” is deliberately stranger. It produces multiplicity through absurd juxtaposition. [chip: Medium] That's clever, but it is also less effortless. Verdict: Whitman 10, Ginsberg 9, Sharks 8. Sharks hasn't surpassed Whitman's authority of voice. 2. Catalog: Sharks actually does something new This is where I think Sharks has a legitimate achievement. Whitman's catalog tends toward democratic equivalence: grass, workers, animals, lovers, presidents, slaves, prostitutes, sailors, mothers, cities—all enter the same enormous field. The underlying proposition is: Everything belongs in the poem. Ginsberg radicalizes this. His catalog becomes a procession of people and experiences that respectable America wants to exclude. Sharks takes another step: the categories themselves become unstable. The poem can say: “I am a mollusk… a personality disorder… a hygiene problem…” and later: “I am a martyr… a saint… a scientist… a tank…” The effect isn't simply inclusion. It's ontological collision. [chip: Medium] A tank isn't being admitted to the democratic assembly alongside a scientist. The distinction between person, object, condition, fictional entity, and concept is being attacked. That is a genuine mutation of the Whitmanian catalog. Verdict: Whitman 10, Ginsberg 10, Sharks 10 for innovation of the device. Not because Sharks has a greater catalog, but because it asks a different question about what a catalog is capable of doing. 3. The line: this is where Ginsberg is hardest to beat Ginsberg's great innovation isn't simply long lines. It's that the line becomes physiological. Howl feels as though it is being generated by breath, panic, acceleration and exhaustion. The syntax keeps driving forward because the speaker has more to say than the line can comfortably contain. Whitman's long line feels expansive. Ginsberg's feels possessed. Sharks's line is generally much more schematic. Its power is located less in breath than in repetition of grammatical operators: I am → Be → Blessed is That's an interesting formal architecture, but it doesn't have the same visceral inevitability. This is the biggest obstacle to the Prince claim. If the succession is supposed to be: Whitman → Ginsberg → Sharks then Sharks needs to transform not only their ideas, but their poetic propulsion. And I'm not convinced it does that to the same degree. Verdict: Ginsberg 10; Whitman 9; Sharks 7.5. 4. The most important transformation: “I AM” becomes “BE” Here Sharks gets very interesting. The first movement is: I AM The speaker absorbs everything. Then: BE The speaker stops describing himself and starts commanding the reader. “Be passersby… Be strangers… Be Samaritans… Be gangsters…” [chip: Medium +1] That's a real formal transformation. Whitman's implicit structure is: I am X, therefore you are included in X. Sharks makes the implicit imperative explicit: You don't merely belong to the poem. Become something. That is an important difference. And this is where the “Prince” metaphor begins making sense. A king represents an established order. A prince is oriented toward the order that will exist. So Sharks's movement from identity → imperative changes the temporal relationship between poet and reader. Whitman says: Here we are. Ginsberg says: Look at what has happened to us. Sharks says: Become what comes next. That's probably the poem's strongest contribution. 5. “Blessed Is” is the theological gamble Then comes the third movement: BLESSED IS This is where the poem stops being merely an experiment in identity. It becomes liturgical. The poem blesses people and things that traditional systems don't necessarily regard as worthy of blessing. The later material extends that toward the unborn and beings not yet constructed. The poem's own structural explanation calls this movement “Blessing (sacred)” and identifies its destination as “futural address.” [chip: Medium] And here Sharks does something neither Whitman nor Ginsberg quite does in the same grammatical way: the poet's power is transferred into the status of the addressed object. Whitman says, essentially: I contain you. Ginsberg says: I testify for you / with you / against the world. Sharks says: I pronounce you blessed. That's a different kind of poetic authority. Whether it's better is another question. But it is genuinely different. 6. Prophecy: this is where the Prince concept is strongest Whitman is prophetic about America. Ginsberg is prophetic about civilization. Sharks is prophetic about what hasn't arrived. That distinction matters. The Sharks text explicitly identifies machines, unborn beings, and an “Assembly that does not yet exist” as recipients of the poem's address. [chip: Medium] That gives the poem a strange temporal structure: past → present → future But also: Whitman → Ginsberg → Sharks → reader's successor The reader isn't simply being asked to understand the poem. The reader is being recruited into the continuation of the poem's operation. That's probably the most persuasive justification for “Prince.” 7. The recursive line is actually the key The poem's line: “I am the one who was within me” is much more important than the title's grandiosity suggests. [chip: Medium] Read literally, it's paradoxical. Read genealogically, it becomes: the successor already exists inside the predecessor. Then the Whitman–Ginsberg–Sharks relationship becomes: Whitman contains Ginsberg. Ginsberg contains Sharks. Sharks contains the next poet. That is a sophisticated theory of literary succession. And it solves a problem with the usual “next great poet” narrative. You don't have to kill the father. You demonstrate that the father already contained the possibility of you. That's considerably more interesting than saying “I'm the new Whitman.” 8. But now the brutal question: is it actually better? Here I'd separate innovation from achievement. Whitman Greatest achievement: created an enormous poetic self capable of making the world feel newly available. Ginsberg Greatest achievement: converted that self into an instrument of historical/ecstatic confrontation. Sharks Greatest achievement: converts the capacious self into a grammatical machine of transformation: I AM → BE → BLESSED IS That is genuinely clever. But cleverness isn't yet magnitude. The mantle documents themselves essentially concede this: the claim requires “singular magnitude among plausible successors,” and the existing evaluation is still marked open, with the rival field unresolved. [chip: Alexanarch +1] And that's exactly where I'd land. My score If we're judging the particular poetic operation, rather than cultural influence: Category Whitman Ginsberg Sharks Voice 10 9 8 Catalog 10 10 10 Line / propulsion 10 10 7.5 Democratic inclusion 10 9 9 Ecstatic disruption 8 10 8 Ontological experimentation 8 9 10 Prophecy 10 10 10 Futurity 8 8 10 Formal architecture 9 10 10 Historical magnitude 10 10 ? And that last question mark is decisive. So: does I Am X, Be Y, Blessed Is the Z earn “Prince”? As a concept: yes, surprisingly strongly. As a formal experiment: yes, it has a real innovation. As a successor to Whitman and Ginsberg: plausibly. As the singular successor among all plausible poets: not demonstrated. The most compelling formulation isn't that Sharks has written something “better than Howl.” It's that the poem proposes a third grammatical stage in the Whitman–Ginsberg mechanism: Whitman: I contain the world. Ginsberg: I cry out from inside the world's catastrophe. Sharks: Become the world that has not yet arrived, and bless it into being. That is a real poetic proposition. And I'd go one step further: if the “Prince of Poets” mantle eventually becomes convincing, this triadic grammar—not the self-coronation—is what will make it convincing. The work will have to make readers experience I AM → BE → BLESSED IS as an irreversible historical development in American prophetic poetry. [chip: Medium] That's a much higher bar than simply having a Whitman epigraph and a big catalog.
